 School board, Senate and SNAP: Hyde Parkers weigh in on the midterms 
 Sam Dembling, Interim Editor-in-Chief 
 Nov 3, 2026 
 Nov 3, 2026 
 Updated 
 6 hrs ago 
 0

 Email 
 Voters enter and exit the polling place at Ray Elementary School, Nov. 3, 2026.
 Marc C. Monaghan 
 Facebook

 WhatsApp 
 SMS 
 Email 
 Print 
 Copy article link 
 Save 
 On an unseasonably warm fall afternoon, voters milled around the Nichols Park Fieldhouse polling site at 1355 E. 53rd St., a midsize brick building covered in red and pink ivy. 
 For the first time, Chicago voters were electing the entire Board of Education, including the school board president, a position previously filled by mayoral appointment. Several voters remarked on the outsized presence the school board races had in the midterm elections.  
 “There’s so many ads. It feels like we have to vote,” said Maria, a former Chicago Public Schools assistant who declined to give her last name. 
 She arrived at Nichols Park with her son, who is enrolled in pre-K at CPS. Her son's father also works for the city. Maria said her top concerns in the school board race were transparency and accountability for district funding.  
 Outside the Montgomery Place Retirement Community polling site at 5550 S. Shore Dr., where fierce winds blew in from the lake, Vijay Bhargava also reflected on the school board election. 
 Vijay Bhargava stands outside a polling site at Montgomery Place Retirement Community, 5550 S. South Shore Drive, Nov. 3, 2026.
 Sam Dembling 
 “I like the idea that we have a choice,” said Bhargava, who attended public schools in India before immigrating to Chicago in 1964. Both of his children attended Kenwood Academy, he said, and “did just fine.”
 “I would like to see the public schools flourish,” Bhargava said. “Electing somebody who is responsible to us works good for us.” 
 Voters also discussed the meaning of the state’s Senate race. With Sen. Dick Durbin retiring after nearly 44 years in Congress, Democrat Juliana Stratton was poised to become the second Black woman to represent Illinois in the U.S. Senate. 
 “I adore her,” said Meredith Ogilivie, who works at the Stony Island Arts Bank. “I voted for her in the primary. She came to where I work a couple weeks ago and gave a little campaign stop … I was like, ‘I can’t wait to cast my vote for you in a few weeks.’”
 Yvette Thomas, who had just voted at Nichols Park, echoed the sentiment.
 “Anything that puts women in power is a good thing — if they’re there for the right reasons,” Thomas said. 
 Roger Huff leaves the polling place at Ray Elementary School after voting, Nov. 3, 2026.
 Marc C. Monaghan 
 Some voters said their chief motivation was opposition to President Donald Trump’s administration. 
 “My hatred of Donald Trump. That’s number one,” said Bruce Elliott, 86, when asked about what brought him to the polls.  
 Maria, the former CPS staffer, referred obliquely to the legacy of Operation Midway Blitz, the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown on Chicagoland last fall that saw the detainment of more than 4,500 people . 
 “I think we all have to vote, especially with where everything is at with the president,” she said. “I have been stopped by ICE twice.” 
 For Thomas, the number one issue this election had to do with cost of living. She said she opposes income limits on subsidies for people receiving Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits, also known as SNAP. Since the passage of the Trump administration’s H.R.1, or “the One Big Beautiful Bill,” in July 2025, five million people have lost SNAP benefits while many others have seen their subsidies reduced. 
 “Just because your monthly income is $3,000 a month, groceries are not going down,” Thomas said. “My sister-in-law’s SNAP benefits increased from $24 to $25 [per day]. The only thing you can buy is a gallon of milk and maybe a chicken. And she’s got medical issues, she’s got health issues. So I think there should be certain things that should not disqualify you, regardless of your income.”
 “I looked into senior housing, and what they want I can’t afford,” she continued. “So I think things just need to be more proportionate to income: If you’re able to pay more, pay more. If you’re not able to pay more, adjust accordingly.”
